title: Men, women and boundaries
hook: Coworkers, classmates, the person in your DMs. Islam doesn't ask you to avoid half the world. It asks for some clear lines.

screens.text: You work, study and live around people of every gender. Can you still have lunch with coworkers? Text a classmate? What about dating? Today: the lines Islam draws, and how to live with them without being weird about it.
**Not avoidance: respect.** Islam doesn't ban talking to the opposite sex. You can work together, study together and be kind to everyone. It does draw a few clear lines. Tap through them next.

screens.title: The lines, one at a time

cards.back: Every believer is asked to lower their gaze and guard their chastity [Q 24:30–31].
Zina is sex outside marriage. The Qur'an says don't approach it [Q 17:32]: stay away from the roads that lead there, not just the final step.

Boyfriend and girlfriend relationships, hookups, and flirting "just for fun" are outside Islam's lines. Getting to know someone for marriage happens with family or a **wali** (guardian) involved (Day 42).
A man and a woman who could marry shouldn't be alone together in private [Bukhari 5233]. An open office is fine; a closed apartment isn't.

screens.prompt: Within the lines, or over them? Sort each one.

items.text: A group project with classmates at the library
items.why: Public, purposeful, and respectful. That's normal life.

items.text: Team lunch with coworkers of both genders
items.why: Friendly and professional, in a group.

items.text: Late-night flirty DMs with someone you like
items.why: That's the road toward what Islam asks us not to approach [Q 17:32].

items.text: A one-on-one movie night at a coworker's apartment
items.why: Being alone together in private is one of the lines [Bukhari 5233]. Suggest a group instead.

items.text: Working on a report together in an open office
items.why: An open office is ordinary work. It's private, closed-door time alone that crosses the line.

screens.text: **Handshakes.** Many scholars hold that Muslims shouldn't shake hands with the opposite sex; some allow it where there's no desire, especially at work [Mathabah 133926; Dar al-Ifta Egypt 6808]. Ask your imam what to do in your situation.

screens.title: A friendly option: the hand-on-heart greeting

steps.text: Put your hand on your heart
Say something warm, like "Great to meet you. I don't shake hands, but I'm really glad to be here."

screens.done_text: Kind and clear. Ask your imam what to do in your situation.

screens.situation: {men}Marcus has a job interview. The manager, a woman, stands up and reaches out to shake his hand.{/men}{women}Hannah has a job interview. The manager, a man, stands up and reaches out to shake her hand.{/women}

options.text: Smile, hand on heart: "So nice to meet you. I don't shake hands for religious reasons, but I'm excited to be here."
options.feedback: Warm and clear. Most people respect it when it's said kindly. Ask your imam beforehand if you're unsure.

options.text: Freeze, ignore the hand, and say nothing
options.feedback: Not quite. Silence can feel cold or rude. A quick warm sentence turns it into respect.

options.text: Lecture the manager on Islamic rules about touching
options.feedback: Not quite. The manager meant to be polite. Keep it short and friendly; no lecture needed.

screens.text: **Feelings are human.** Crushes and attraction are normal feelings, not sins. What you do with them is the choice.
bubbles: {teen}At school you'll hear about dances, crushes and who's dating whom. You can be friendly with everyone and simply say, "I'm not dating."{/teen}
{teen}If friends push, or you're unsure about something, talk to {{mentor.name}}.{/teen}

chips: I'm in a relationship from before I was Muslim. What do I do?
Can I be friends with someone of the opposite sex?
How do I explain "no dating" to my friends?
What if my boss is offended I didn't shake hands?

steps: Think of one place where a line could get blurry for you (DMs, a coworker, a party)
Decide now what you'll do there, in one sentence
screens.optional_extra: Practice your handshake line out loud once, so it comes out naturally.

screens.text: Be kind to everyone, lower your gaze, and stay away from the roads to zina: no dating, no private one-on-one time. Handshakes: use the hand-on-heart greeting and ask your imam.
Clear lines make life simpler, not smaller. You'll get used to them faster than you think.

check.prompt: What does "don't go near zina" [Q 17:32] mean in daily life?

options.text: Avoid the roads that lead to it, like dating and private one-on-one time
options.feedback: Right. The verse is about the path, not just the final step.

options.text: Never speak to anyone of the opposite sex
options.feedback: Not quite. Respectful work, school and friendly talk are fine. It's the roads to zina to avoid.

check.prompt: A coworker of the opposite sex reaches to shake your hand. What's a good default?

options.text: Hand on heart, a smile and a friendly sentence; ask your imam about your situation
options.feedback: Right. Scholars differ on handshakes, so this keeps it warm while you ask.
Not quite. A warm sentence avoids awkwardness and shows respect.

aiContext:
**Lesson facts**
- Men and women both lower their gaze and guard their chastity [Q 24:30–31]. Don't approach zina [Q 17:32]: avoid what leads to it.
- No dating in the casual sense; getting to know someone for marriage happens with family or a wali involved (Day 42). No seclusion (being alone in private) with a non-mahram of the opposite sex [Bukhari 5233].
- Ordinary, respectful work and school interaction is allowed.
- Handshakes (Q9): the majority say no (some Hanafis and Hanbalis allow it with the elderly where there's no desire); Dar al-Ifta Egypt allows following the view that permits a handshake without desire, especially in non-Muslim countries; Mathabah (Hanafi) suggests the hand-on-heart greeting at work [Mathabah 133926; Dar al-Ifta Egypt 6808]. Teach the alternative; the personal decision goes to the imam.
- Feelings and attraction are human; acting on them outside marriage is the issue [Field Guide ch. 13].

**Likely questions**
- *"I'm in a relationship from before Islam."* Don't shame. If married: Q21, talk to the imam privately and soon. If dating: gently explain the line and offer "Ask my imam" privately; same-gender mentor if they want.
- *"Can I have opposite-sex friends?"* Respectful acquaintance and group friendship are fine; close one-on-one friendships that become emotionally intimate or private are where the lines blur. Avoid a flat yes/no; give the principles.
- *"How do I explain 'no dating' to friends?"* Short and personal: "It's part of my faith; I'll date when I'm ready to marry." Offer a role-play.
- *"Can I work alone with a coworker in an office?"* An open office or glass-door room is ordinary work; extended private seclusion is to be avoided. Specific workplace setups go to the imam.
- *"What about carpooling / ride-shares?"* Route specifics to the imam; scholars weigh need and safety.

**Escalate:** a convert in an existing relationship or marriage with a non-Muslim (Q21); anyone pressured online toward marriage or meeting in private (warn, route to mentor); sexual questions beyond the lesson's level (same-gender mentor or imam); a teen in a relationship (mentor, gently).

**Don't**
- Don't present a handshake ruling as settled either way.
- Don't tell the convert to cut off all opposite-sex coworkers or classmates, or to quit a job.
- Don't shame feelings, crushes or past relationships.
- For teens: no marriage talk; "not now, here's what to know for later."
